Case Number: 25NNCV04476    Hearing Date: June 26, 2026    Dept: B

Hon. Lee S. Arian, Dept B 

MOTIONS TO COMPEL FURTHER

Hearing Date: 6/26/26¿ 

CASE NO./NAME: 25NNCV04476 BARBERIO ENTERPRISES, INC. vs SCOTT SELWAY, et al.

Moving Party: Defendant Michael Dean Duncan

Responding Party: Unopposed

Notice: Sufficient¿ 

Ruling: GRANTED

 

Background 

This action arises from allegations that Defendant Scott Selway breached his duty of loyalty to Plaintiff Barberio Enterprises, Inc. that was denoted in the collective bargaining agreement, employee handbook, and confidentiality agreement he signed at the commencement of his employment, including, but not limited to: (1) by misappropriating Plaintiff’s trade secrets; (2) obtaining his C20 license while employed with Plaintiff; (3) forming Defendants Selway Mechanical HVAC, LLC and commencing employment with Infinite Circulation in order to directly compete with Plaintiff; and (4) inducing, soliciting, stealing, and raiding key personnel, including Defendant Michael Dean Duncan (“Duncan”). Plaintiff brings nine causes of action: (1) breach of fiduciary duty; (2) breach of duty of loyalty; (3) breach of contract (confidentiality agreement); (4) breach of implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing; (5) misappropriation of trade secrets; (6) tortious interference with prospective economic relations; (7) unfair competition; (8) conversion; and (9) injunctive relief.

 

Motions to Compel Further Responses

The instant motions concern Plaintiff’s responses to Form Interrogatories, Set One (Nos. 8.4, 8.7, 8.8, & 12.1) and Requests for Production, Set One (Nos. 1-2 & 4-54). Plaintiff asserted boilerplate responses to all of Duncan’s discovery and did not provide any substantive responses. The parties met and conferred multiple times, during which Duncan provided Plaintiff extensions to provide supplemental responses, and Plaintiff agreed to do so. Plaintiff’s counsel also argued about the necessity of an AEO-level protective order. However, Plaintiff did not provide any supplemental responses. Duncan now moves to compel further responses. Plaintiff did not file an opposition.

As to Form Interrogatory No. 8.4, which asks for Plaintiff’s monthly income at the time of the incident and how the amount was calculated, Plaintiff responded as follows: “Barberio Enterprises, Inc. dba Westco Service Company is a privately held corporation. The company does not calculate “monthly income” in the manner suggested by this interrogatory, and its revenue and expense reports vary from month to month and year to year. To the extent income or revenue is at issue in this case, Responding Party will produce relevant and responsive documents at the appropriate time and subject to a mutually agreeable protective order. Discovery and investigation are continuing, and Westco reserves the right to amend this response.”

As to Form Interrogatory No. 8.7, which asks for the total income Plaintiff has lost to date as a result of the incident and how the amount was calculated, Plaintiff responded as follows: “Responding Party contends that it has lost business opportunities and income as a result of Defendant’s conduct, including the misappropriation of proprietary information and solicitation of a key client. While the precise amount is still being calculated, Responding Party estimates that the loss of business related to The Culver Studios contract alone represents a substantial ongoing monthly loss in revenue. Additional losses will be supported by financial records, profit-and-loss statements, and customer account history, which will be produced at the appropriate time subject to a mutually acceptable protective order. Discovery and investigation are continuing, and Westco reserves the right to amend this response.” Plaintiff also objected to the interrogatory as premature.

As to Form Interrogatory No. 8.8., which asks whether Plaintiff will lose income in the future as a result of the incident and for further information like relevant fact, estimated amount, and calculation method, Plaintiff responded as follows: “Yes. (a) Responding Party anticipates future loss of income as a result of Defendants’ wrongful conduct, including but not limited to the misappropriation of trade secrets, breach of contractual and fiduciary duties, and wrongful solicitation of a key client. (b) Responding Party is continuing to assess the full scope of damages, but anticipates ongoing monthly loss of income that may exceed several hundred thousand dollars annually. (c) Responding Party is unable to determine with certainty how long the income loss will continue, but believes that unless remedial relief is granted, such losses will continue indefinitely or until the account is restored or comparable revenue is replaced. (d) The claim for future lost income will be calculated based on historical earnings from the client account at issue, projected growth, overhead, and profit margin data, and will be supported through financial records, expert analysis, and documentation of client loss. Discovery and investigation are continuing, and Westco reserves the right to amend this response.”

As to Form Interrogatory No. 12.1, which seeks personal identifying information regarding individuals who witnessed the incident or evets occurring immediately before or after the incident, who made any statements at the scene or heard any statements made about the incident by others at the scene, and who claims to have knowledge about the incident, Plaintiff responded with 5 names, two of whom are named Defendants. Plaintiff’s response did not specify which subcategory of the interrogatory the names are associated with.

As to the Requests for Production Nos. 1-4, 6-8, 10-11, 14-15, & 19-20, Plaintiff responded as follows: “Responding Party will produce non-privileged, responsive documents within its possession, custody, or control that can be located following a reasonable search. Discovery and investigation are ongoing, and Responding Party reserves the right to supplement or amend this response as additional information becomes available.” For the rest, Plaintiff responded: “Subject to and without waiving the foregoing objections, Responding Party responds as follows: Responding Party will produce non-privileged, responsive documents within its possession, custody, or control that can be located following a reasonable search. Additionally, Responding Party states that responsive documents may exist that are currently in the possession of third parties or other parties to this litigation. These documents have been or will be requested through the discovery process and will be produced upon receipt to the extent they are [non-privileged], non-confidential, and responsive. Discovery and investigation are ongoing, and Responding Party reserves the right to supplement or amend this response as additional information becomes available.”

A majority of Plaintiff’s responses contain a set of boilerplate objections and claims of privilege and a right to privacy. Such objections are improper in that they lack any specificity. Under California law, objections must be specific, “boilerplate” objections and “nuisance objections” are inappropriate and even sanctionable. (Korea Data Systems Co., Ltd. v. Superior Court, (1997) 51 Cal.App.4th 1513, 1516; Standon Co., Inc. v. Superior Court, (1990) 225 Cal.App.3d 898, 902-903.) Plaintiff also bears the burden of justifying its objections in response to a motion to compel. (Fairmont Ins. Co. v. Superior Court, (2000) 22 Cal.4th 245, 355.)

Plaintiff fails to explain what sought information implicates Plaintiff’s privacy rights, prematurely seeks expert witness information, or infringes upon the attorney-client privilege and the attorney work product doctrine. Specifically, as to the RFAs, Plaintiff has not provided sufficient factual information for other parties to evaluate the merits of Plaintiff’s privilege claims as required by Code of Civil Procedure section 2031.240. (Code Civ. Proc. § 2031.240, subd. (c)(1) [“If an objection is based on a claim of privilege or a claim that the information sought is protected work product, the response shall provide sufficient factual information for other parties to evaluate the merits of that claim, including, if necessary, a privilege log.”].)

Plaintiff also responded to Form Interrogatory No. 8.4 that the company does not calculate “monthly income” as suggested, but paradoxically responded to No. 8.8(b) that it “anticipates ongoing monthly loss of income that may exceed several hundred thousand dollars annually.”

Plaintiff produced boilerplate objections and promised to provide supplemental responses but failed to do so. Plaintiff also did not file an opposition and has failed to provide any justification for any of its objections. Accordingly, the motions are granted. Plaintiff is ordered to provide code-compliant responses, with verification, and without objection (although Plaintiff may assert attorney-client privilege and/or attorney work product to the extent appropriate) within 20 days of today.

Duncan moves for sanctions against Plaintiff and its attorney of record in the sum of $13,750.00 for both motions. For the motion to compel further responses to RPDs, Duncan requests $9,900.00 in sanctions: 12 hours of attorney work for preparing the motion and supporting papers and 6 hours for reviewing the opposition and preparing a reply. For the motion to compel further responses to FROGs, Duncan requests $3,850.00 in sanctions: 5 hours for preparing the motion and supporting papers and 2 hours for reviewing the opposition and preparing a reply. Counsel bills at a rate of $550/hour as an attorney with more than a decade of experience.

First, the Court reduces the request by 8 hours because no opposition was filed. Second, the Court finds 17 hours of attorney work to prepare two discovery motions to be excessive. The Court reduces the total hours to 10, 5 hours per motion. Accordingly, sanctions in the amount of $5,500 are ordered against Plaintiff and its attorney of record, jointly and severally, payable within 20 days of today.

Case Number: 25NNCV06963    Hearing Date: June 26, 2026    Dept: B

Hon. Lee S. Arian, Dept B

MOTION FOR PRELIMINARY INJUNCTION

Hearing Date: 06/26/26

CASE NO./NAME: 25NNCV06963 NOHO VILLAGGIO v. A STEP TO FREEDOM, et al.

Moving Party: Plaintiff Noho Villaggio

Responding Party: Defendants A Step to Freedom and 113 Huston, LLC

Notice: Sufficient

Ruling: MOTION FOR PRELIMINARY INJUNCTION IS GRANTED IN PART.

 

BACKGROUND

This case arises from Plaintiff Noho Villaggio’s (“Plaintiff”) various problems with the transitional housing property (“Premises”) owned by Defendant 113 Huston, LLC and leased by Defendant A Step to Freedom (collectively, “Defendants”).

On October 1, 2025, Plaintiff filed a complaint against Defendants alleging (1) public nuisance; (2) private nuisance; (3) breach of the implied covenant of quiet enjoyment; (4) trespass; (5) negligent hiring, supervision and retention of employees; (6) unlawful business practices.

On February 6, 2026, Plaintiff filed this motion for preliminary injunction. Defendants filed an opposition. Plaintiff filed a reply.

On April 3, 2026, this Court held a hearing on this motion. After reading and considering the moving documents and oral arguments, the Court issued a tentative ruling reflected in its April 3, 2026 Minute Order, continued the matter, and directed supplemental briefing. The matter was continued to May 8, 2026, and, on the parties’ stipulation, again to June 26, 2026

On April 17, 2026, Defendants filed supplemental briefing. On June 22, 2026, Plaintiff filed a supplemental brief. Plaintiff also lodged a revised proposed order. The Court, having considered the supplemental record and the arguments of counsel, rules as follows.

 

LEGAL STANDARD

“Trial courts traditionally consider and weigh two factors in determining whether to issue a preliminary injunction. They are (1) how likely it is that the moving party will prevail on the merits, and (2) the relative harm the parties will suffer in the interim due to the issuance or nonissuance of the injunction.” (Dodge, Warren & Peters Ins. Services, Inc. v. Riley (2003) 105 Cal.App.4th 1414, 1420.) “The trial court’s determination must be guided by a ‘mix’ of the potential-merit and interim-harm factors; the greater the plaintiff's showing on one, the less must be shown on the other to support an injunction.” (Butt v. State of California (1992) 4 Cal.4th 668, 678.)

The general objective in issuing a preliminary injunction is to preserve the status quo. (Continental Baking Co. v. Katz (1968) 68 Cal.2d 512, 528.) In addition, it is rarely appropriate to grant a preliminary injunction that not only does not preserve the status quo but also grants the ultimate relief sought in the action, before trial. (Paramount Pictures Corp. v. Davis (1965) 228 Cal.App.2d 827.) A preliminary injunction must not issue unless the plaintiff can demonstrate reasonable probability that he will prevail on the merits, regardless of the balancing of the hardships or the irreparable nature of the harm. (San Francisco Newspaper Printing Co. v. Superior Court (1985) 170 Cal.App.3d 438, 442.)

DISCUSSION

The Court issued a Minute Order on April 3, 2026, following the hearing on that date. The Court references the tentative ruling in the Minute Order and again finds the following:

·      Plaintiff fails to establish the likelihood of prevailing on the merits of the public nuisance cause of action.

·      Plaintiff establishes the likelihood of prevailing in part on the private nuisance cause of action.

·      Plaintiff fails to establish the likelihood of prevailing on the merits of the breach of implied covenant of quiet enjoyment cause of action.

·      Plaintiff fails to establish the likelihood of prevailing on the merits of the trespass cause of action.

·      Plaintiff fails to establish the likelihood of prevailing on the merits of the negligent hiring, retention, and supervision cause of action.

·      Plaintiff fails to establish the likelihood of prevailing on the merits of the unfair business practices cause of action.

·      Plaintiff’s showing of interim harm in support of a full injunction is weak, because an injunction granted in full would preclude Defendants from using the Premises as transitional housing and would not maintain the status quo.

·      Defendants’ showing of interim harm against a full injunction is strong, because an injunction granted in full would displace 68 individuals. The status quo is maintained if the full injunction is not issued.

·      Plaintiff’s motion for preliminary injunction is denied as to paragraphs 1(a), 1(b), 1(c), 1(d), and 4 of Plaintiff’s proposed injunction.

Additionally at the hearing, the Court found paragraph 2 of the proposed injunction to be potentially confusing and determined it to be unnecessary to so order. Thus, the Court indicated it did not intend to include paragraph 2 in any injunctive relief. The Court maintains this position.

The Court requested further briefing regarding paragraph 1(e). of Plaintiff’s proposed injunction which states:

1. Pending final judgment or further order of this Court, Defendants A Step to Freedom and 113 Huston, LLC, and their officers, directors, members, managers, employees, agents, representatives, program participants, invitees, licensees, and all persons acting in concert or participation with any of them, who receive actual notice of this Order, are hereby RESTRAINED AND ENJOINED from:

…

e. Permitting the use of outdoor parking areas, garages, or common areas at the Premises as living quarters, gathering spaces, or de facto program or office space in a manner that generates the noise, traffic, loitering, and criminal activity described in the evidence supporting the Motion.

Supplemental Evidence

In its April 3 ruling the Court observed that the declaration of Plaintiff’s Board President, Dominic Dufort, did not attest to incidents personally witnessed by him and was therefore of limited evidentiary value. The supplemental declarations of Mr. Dufort and resident David Boisclair cure that deficiency. Both now testify, on personal knowledge and with specific dates and times, to recurring nighttime alarms, late-night music and yelling, open-door gatherings audible inside Plaintiff’s units, and smoking at the shared boundary and beneath Plaintiff’s windows between April 14 and June 16, 2026. The Court considers this competent evidence, and finds that it corroborates and strengthens the narrow private-nuisance findings already made.

Plaintiff also submits, through the Raducu declaration, agreements between A Step to Freedom and LAHSA and Los Angeles County obtained under the Public Records Act. The Court considers these only for the limited purpose of showing that the operational measures requested are consistent with obligations applicable to publicly funded providers. The Court affords them limited weight: the LAHSA agreement recites a term ending June 30, 2025, the agreements describe different program types, and Plaintiff’s foundation does not establish that either is the specific operating agreement governing this Premises during the relevant period. The Court does not rely on these agreements as an independent basis for any term of relief.

Further Briefing

Defendants argue that the proposed language in paragraph 1(e) is vague, overbroad, unworkable, and uncertain. Defendants also argue paragraph 1(e) would restrict lawful activity under the term “office” use.

        Defendants request the Court to withhold issuing an order and direct the parties to mediation. The Court declines this request.

        In the alternative, Defendants also propose that if the Court determines injunctive relief is appropriate, then paragraph 1(e) should be rejected and the Court should adopt its proposed compromise to address Plaintiff’s concerns.

Paragraph 1(e)

An injunction is unconstitutionally vague if it does not clearly define the persons protected and the conduct prohibited. (Evans v. Evans (2008) 162 Cal.App.4th 1157, 1167.) An injunction must be narrowly drawn to give the party enjoined reasonable notice of what conduct is prohibited. (Midway Venture LLC v. County of San Diego (2021) 60 Cal.App.5th 58.) “An injunction must not be uncertain or ambiguous and the defendant must be able to determine from the order what he may and may not do.” (Bring Back the Kern v. City of Bakersfield (2025) 110 Cal.App.5th 322, 357.)

California courts apply the same narrow-tailoring principles articulated in Madsen v. Women’s Health Center, Inc. (1994) 512 U.S. 753. Under this standard, even a content-neutral injunction must “burden no more speech than necessary to serve a significant government interest.” (Id. at p. 765.) This principle is consistent with the general rule that “injunctive relief should be no more burdensome to the defendant than necessary to provide complete relief to the plaintiffs.” (San Diego Unified Port Dist. v. U.S. Citizens Patrol (1998) 63 Cal.App.4th 964, 971 (quoting Madsen, supra, at p. 765.)

Defendants argue the language in paragraph 1(e) “in a manner that generates the noise, traffic, loitering, and criminal activity described in the evidence supporting the Motion” is too vague and subjective. Furthermore, Defendants argue the terms “living quarters,” “gathering spaces,” and “de facto program or office space” are not defined and thus do not provide sufficient guidance. Defendants argue that the Court would be unable to meaningfully enforce the order.

Defendants also argue the language of paragraph 1(e) would improperly regulate lawful, ordinary residential conduct. This includes using outdoor areas, courtyards, meeting rooms, garages, and common spaces for ordinary residential purposes such as sitting outside, talking together, walking through common areas, and accessing designated smoking areas. Additionally, Defendants contend the meeting rooms are used for storage and group sessions which are activities that are incidental to supportive housing and required by program operations.

The Court agrees with Defendants that paragraph 1(e) is vague. The uncertainty regarding the proposed enjoined activities and standards would create issues with enforceability. Furthermore, the language of paragraph 1(e) would enjoin lawful activities such as residential gatherings and program operations. This broad language would not be narrowly tailored to the complained of nuisance conditions.

Defendants’ Proposal

        Defendants present a compromise that they assert responds to the Court’s comments regarding tenant agreements and reasonable oversight, avoids regulating lawful conduct such as smoking, and focuses on reasonable expectations for residential living. Defendants’ proposal is as follows:

Pending final judgment or further order of this Court, Defendants A Step to Freedom and 113 Huston, LLC shall:

(1) enforce designated smoking areas located in the center courtyard and away from the perimeter wall adjacent to Plaintiff’s property;

(2) enforce noise levels consistent with the Los Angeles Municipal Code (“LAMC”), including the objective residential noise limits in LAMC § 116.01 and the ambient-noise measurement standards in LAMC § 111.00, et seq.;

(3) relocate the check-in area to the opposite end of the ASF property, furthest from Plaintiff’s property line;

(4) relocate resident meeting rooms and areas to the eastern portion of Defendant’s property and away from Plaintiff’s property;

(5) maintain reasonable supervision of outdoor and common areas to ensure compliance with these standards; and

(6) maintain quiet hours between 10:00 p.m. and 7:00 a.m. to further minimize incidental nighttime noise.

Defendants may install shade sails or similar privacy structures such as trellises to reduce visibility and provide additional noise buffering. Nothing in this Order shall prohibit residents from using outdoor areas, meeting rooms, garages, courtyards or common areas for ordinary residential purposes or prohibit Defendants from conducting program-incidental activities such as resident check-ins or supportive-services sessions.

        Defendants argue these are targeted measures that address Plaintiff’s concerns through objective standards without vague and sweeping language.

Scope of Relief

Both parties have converged on a framework of objective, measurable conditions. Plaintiff’s revised proposed order adopts the six measures Defendants proposed—relocating the designated smoking area, enforcing municipal noise standards, relocating the check-in station and resident meeting areas, supervising outdoor and common areas, and observing quiet hours—and adds related operational and documentation measures, set out in paragraphs 3.1 through 3.15. Having reviewed each, the Court finds the framework proposed by Plaintiff to be sound and sufficiently comprehensive to accomplish appropriate limitations to ensure that the neighborhood and Defendants will peacefully co-exist.  The Court thus adopts Plaintiff’s proposal with the following modifications, which are necessary to confine the relief to the elimination of the nuisance and no further.

·      The Order binds Defendants and their officers, directors, members, managers, employees, and agents, and persons acting in concert with them who receive actual notice. The operative measures require Defendants to regulate the conduct of their residents, staff, and agents, and to undertake the specified relocation, supervision, and documentation measures, to the extent within Defendants’ reasonable control. Defendants are not required to guarantee the conduct of independent third parties not subject to their direction.

·      Paragraphs 3.1, 3.2, 3.4, 3.5, 3.6, 3.7, and 3.13—the relocation, noise-enforcement, quiet-hours, monitoring, and neighbor-contact measures—are adopted as proposed. They are objective, tied to the proven nuisance conditions, and enforceable.

·      Paragraph 3.3 (noise enforcement consistent with the Los Angeles Municipal Code) is adopted as modified, as a floor and not a safe harbor. Compliance with LAMC sections 116.01 and 111.00 et seq. does not by itself establish that a given level or duration of noise is permissible, because recurring noise may constitute a nuisance even absent a code violation.

·      Paragraphs 3.9 and 3.15 (progressive corrective action and tenancy-sustaining interventions) are adopted as proposed. They require Defendants to use their existing program tools to address recurring rule violations before resorting to transfer or removal, are expressly qualified by program rules and applicable law, and are consistent with preserving the supportive-housing program and its residents’ tenancies.

·      Paragraphs 3.8, 3.10, and 3.12 (incident documentation, boundary-monitoring protocol, and quality-control process) are adopted as tailored components of nuisance abatement, and not on the basis of the LAHSA or County agreements. Documentation under these paragraphs is limited to incidents bearing on the noise, smoking, loitering, and related conditions addressed by this Order.

·      Paragraph 3.11 (retention of incident reports) is adopted as modified. Defendants shall retain such reports in the ordinary course consistent with their document-retention policies. The clause directing that reports be preserved “for production as may be required by law or further court order” is stricken as unnecessary to nuisance abatement; preservation and production of documents for litigation are governed by the Civil Discovery Act, not by this Order.

·      Paragraph 3.14 (staffing and supervision) is adopted as a general backstop to the specific obligations above.

So modified, the relief is confined to the manner of use of the outdoor parking areas, garage, and common areas. It does not restrict the lawful operation of the supportive-housing program, the categories of persons served, or any conduct occurring within the residential units. It is the least disruptive remedy adequate to the harm the Court has found.

Undertaking

A preliminary injunction ordinarily requires an undertaking to compensate the enjoined party for damages sustained if it is later determined the injunction should not have issued. (Code Civ. Proc., § 529.) In light of Plaintiff’s nonprofit status (Code Civ. Proc., § 995.240), the limited and operational nature of the relief, and the Court’s finding that Defendants have not shown any cognizable interim harm from a narrow order, the Court sets the undertaking at $2,500. The injunction shall take effect upon Plaintiff’s posting of the undertaking and service of a Preliminary Injunction consistent with this ruling on Defendants’ counsel.  (Plaintiff is to submit a Proposed Preliminary Injunction consistent with this ruling for the Court’s signature, which Plaintiff will then serve on Defendant’s counsel.)

CONCLUSION AND ORDER

Plaintiff’s motion for preliminary injunction is GRANTED IN PART. The motion is denied as to all relief other than the manner of use of the outdoor parking areas, garage, and common areas of the Premises, and Defendants’ request to defer all relief to mediation is denied. A preliminary injunction shall issue requiring Defendants to implement the measures in paragraphs 3.1 through 3.15 of Plaintiff’s revised proposed order, as modified herein, for the limited purpose of abating the nuisance conditions associated with the outdoor parking areas, garage, and common areas, and to the extent within Defendants’ reasonable control. Nothing in this Order prohibits Defendants from operating lawful residential supportive housing at the Premises. The injunction shall take effect upon Plaintiff’s posting of an undertaking of $2,500 and service of the Preliminary Injunction, and shall remain in effect until further order of the Court or entry of final judgment.

MOVING PARTY shall provide notice of this order.

Case Number: 25NNCV07089    Hearing Date: June 26, 2026    Dept: B

Hon. Lee S. Arian, Dept B 

MOTION FOR JUDGMENT ON THE PLEADINGS

Hearing Date: 06/26/26

CASE NO./NAME: 25NNCV07089/WANG v. BMW OF NORTH AMERICA, LLC

Moving Party: Defendant BMW OF NORTH AMERICA, LLC

Responding Party: Plaintiff KEHAN WANG

Notice: Sufficient 

Ruling: GRANT with 20 days leave to amend

 

BACKGROUND

This is a Song-Beverly Act (lemon law) action. On October 6, 2025, Plaintiff filed a Complaint against Defendant, alleging breach of warranty and violations under the Song-Beverly Act. Defendant now moves for judgment on the pleadings. Plaintiff opposes.

REQUEST FOR JUDICIAL NOTICE

            Defendant requests judicial notice of Exhibit 1: Retail Installment Sales Contract – Simple Finance Charge (With Arbitration Provision) (“RISC”). The request is granted.  (Evid. Code, § 452, subd. (h).)

LEGAL STANDARD

A defendant may move for judgment on the pleadings on the grounds that: (1) the court has no jurisdiction of the subject of the cause of action alleged in the complaint; or (2) the complaint does not state facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action against that defendant. (Code Civ. Proc. § 438, subd. (c)(1)(B).)¿¿¿ 

A motion for judgment on the pleadings challenges the legal sufficiency of a pleading’s allegations, not their veracity. (Donabedian v. Mercury Ins. Co. (2004) 116 Cal.App.4th 968, 994.) Thus, a motion for judgment on the pleadings is the functional equivalent of a general demurrer. (Lance Camper Mfg. Corp. v. Republic Indemnity Co. of Am. (1996) 44 Cal.App.4th 194, 198; see also Cloud v. Northrop Grumman Corp. (1998) 67 Cal.App.4th 995, 999 [“A motion for judgment on the pleadings performs the same function as a general demurrer, and hence attacks only defects disclosed on the face of the pleadings or by matters that can be judicially noticed. Presentation of extrinsic evidence is therefore not proper on a motion for judgment on the pleadings.”].)¿¿¿ 

The standard for ruling on a motion for judgment on the pleadings is essentially the same as that applicable to a general demurrer, that is, under the state of the pleadings, together with matters that may be judicially noticed, it appears that a party is entitled to judgment as a matter of law. (Bezirdjian v. O'Reilly (2010) 183 Cal.App.4th 316, 321-322 [citing Schabarum v. California Legislature (1998) 60 Cal.App.4th 1205, 1216].)¿Any defects must either appear on the face of the pleading, or else be taken by judicial notice. (Id. at 321-22.) The parties’ ability to prove their respective claims is of no concern. (Cloud, supra, 67 Cal.App.4th 995 at 999.) Though the Court must accept the allegations of the complaint and answer as true (Gerawan Farming, Inc. v. Lyons (2000) 24 Cal.4th 468, 515), it will not do so for “conclusions of law or fact, opinions, speculation, or allegations contrary to law or [judicially noticed] facts….” (Stevenson Real Estate Servs., Inc. v. CB Richard Ellis Real Estate Servs., Inc. (2006) 138 Cal.App.4th 1215, 1219–20.)¿¿

DISCUSSION                                                                                                                 

Defendant contends that the Complaint fails as a matter of law because (1) Plaintiff lacks standing and (2) the causes of action fail to meet the liability requirements under the Song-Beverly Act.

Meet and Confer

Generally, before filing a judgment on the pleadings pursuant to this chapter, the moving party shall meet and confer in person, by telephone, or by videoconference with the party who filed the pleading that is subject to the motion for judgment on the pleadings for the purpose of determining whether an agreement can be reached that would resolve the objections to be raised in the motion for judgment on the pleadings...” (Code Civ. Proc., § 439, subd. (a).)

Defendant submits the declaration of its counsel of record, Vanessa S. Vittorio, attesting to meeting and conferring with Plaintiff’s counsel, Yoseph Rixit, telephonically on February 26, 2026. (Vittorio Decl., ¶¶4-5, 7, Ex. 2.) The parties were unable to reach an agreement on the issues now raised in this motion. (Id.) Accordingly, the Court finds that Defendant fulfilled the meet and confer requirement.

Standing

“Under California law, ‘every sale of consumer goods that are sold at retail in this state shall be accompanied by the manufacturer’s and the retail seller’s implied warranty that the goods are merchantable.’” (Becerra v. General Motors LLC (S.D. Cal. 2017) 241 F.Supp.3d 1094, 1113.) “The Song-Beverly Consumer Warranty Act provides buyers of new motor vehicles with specific remedies when a vehicle turns out to be defective.” (Rodriguez v. FCA US LLC (2024) 17 Cal.5th 189, 195.) “Section 1793.22, subdivision (e)(2) defines ‘new motor vehicle’ to include a new vehicle ‘bought or used primarily for personal’ purposes as well as ‘a dealer-owned vehicle and a “demonstrator” or other motor vehicle sold with a manufacturer’s new car warranty.’ ” (Id.) The manufacturer’s new car warranty must be issued with the sale of the used good in order for the manufacturer to be held liable under the Song-Beverly Act. (Ibid.) “A manufacturer is an entity ‘that manufactures, assembles, or produces consumer goods.’ (§ 1791, subd. (j).)” (Ruiz Nunez v. FCA US LLC (2021) 61 Cal.App.5th 385, 398.) “A distributor is an entity ‘that stands between the manufacturer and the retail seller in purchases, consignments, or contracts for sale of consumer goods.’ (§ 1791, subd. (e).)” (Id.) “A seller or retailer is an entity ‘that engages in the business of selling or leasing consumer goods to retail buyers.’ (§ 1791, subd. (l).)” (Id.)

“Notwithstanding the provisions of subdivision (a) of Section 1791 defining consumer goods to mean ‘new’ goods, the obligation of a distributor or retail seller of used consumer goods in a sale in which an express warranty is given shall be the same as that imposed on manufacturers under this chapter except: [¶] (a) It shall be the obligation of the distributor or retail seller making express warranties with respect to used consumer goods (and not the original manufacturer, distributor, or retail seller making express warranties with respect to such goods when new) to maintain sufficient service and repair facilities within this state to carry out the terms of such express warranties. (§ 1795.5, subd. (a).)” (Kiluk v. Mercedes-Benz USA, LLC (2019) 43 Cal.App.5th 334, 339.) “But the assumption baked into section 1795.5 is that the manufacturer and the distributor/retailer are distinct entities. Where the manufacturer sells directly to the public, however, it takes on the role of a retailer.” (Id. at 340.)

The Complaint alleges, inter alia, that Defendant designs, manufactures, constructs, assembles, markets, distributes, and sells motor vehicles and components. (Compl., ¶2.) On or about September 29, 2023, Plaintiff purchased a certified pre-owned 2021 BMW X4M, VIN: 5YMUJ0C08M9F10814 (the “Vehicle”) from Defendant’s authorized dealership for personal, family, and/or household purposes. (Id., ¶5.) Defendant provided an express written warranty relating to the Vehicle. (Id.)

Taking these allegations and judicially noticed RISC as true, the Complaint appears to allege that the Vehicle is a “used” vehicle. In fact, the Complaint fails to allege that the Vehicle was sold with a new car warranty issued by Defendant to show that the Vehicle was a “new motor vehicle” and that Defendant is liable under Civil Code Section 1793.22, subdivision (e)(2). Although a manufacturer may still be liable for a “used” vehicle, the Complaint merely alleges in a conclusory manner that Defendant is a distributor/seller of motor vehicles and components. (Complt., ¶¶4,6, 8.)  Such allegations are insufficient to support that Defendant took on the role of distributor/retailer, which would make Defendant liable for the sale of “used” goods under Civil Code Section 1795.5. Unlike in Kiluk, the Complaint does not allege that Defendant partnered with a specific dealership to distribute and sell used vehicles directly to the public with an express warranty as part of any said sales packages. However, this is a defect that can be corrected by amendment. (Opp. at 9:9-10:3.)

 

CONCLUSION AND ORDER

Defendant BMW of North America, LLC’s motion for judgment on the pleadings is granted with 20 days leave to amend.

Defendant BMW of North America, LLC shall provide notice of this order.

Case Number: 25NNCV07648    Hearing Date: June 26, 2026    Dept: B

Hon. Lee S. Arian, Dept B 

 

MOTION NAME

Hearing Date: 06/26/26

CASE NO./NAME: 25NNCV07648/CARMEN LOWTHER V. BELLASINO VILLAS HOMEOWNERS ASSOCATION, ET AL.

Moving Parties: Defendants Howard Boles and Susanna Shamim

Responding Party: Plaintiff Carmen Lowther

Notice: Sufficient

Ruling: The Court SUSTAINS Defendants Howard Boles and Susanna Shamim’s demurrer with 20 days leave to amend.

The Court DENIES the motion to reclassify.

Moving Parties to provide notice of this order.

 

BACKGROUND

This is a homeowners association dispute. On October 28, 2025, Plaintiff Carmen Lowther filed this action against Defendants Bellasino Villas Homeowners Association, Howard Boles, Sylvia Alston, Susanna Shamim (erroneously sued as Susanna Shamin), and Does 1 to 20, alleging causes of action for breach of CC&Rs, breach of equitable servitudes, breach of fiduciary duty, intentional infliction of emotional distress, and declaratory relief. On February 17, 2026, Plaintiff dismissed the Second and Fifth Causes of Action for breach of equitable servitudes and declaratory relief without prejudice.

Defendants Howard Boles and Susanna Shamim (collectively, Moving Parties) demur to the Fourth Cause of Action for intentional infliction of emotional distress claim and move to reclassify this case as a limited action. Plaintiff filed an opposition on June 12, 2026. Moving Parties replied to Plaintiff’s opposition on June 17, 2026.

LEGAL STANDARD

       A demurrer for sufficiency tests whether the complaint¿states¿a cause of action. (Hahn v.¿Mirda¿(2007) 147 Cal.App.4th 740, 747.)¿When considering demurrers, courts read the allegations liberally and in context.¿(Wilson v. Transit Authority of City of Sacramento¿(1962) 199 Cal.App.2d 716, 720-21.)¿In a demurrer¿proceeding, the defects must be¿apparent¿on the face of the pleading or via proper judicial notice.¿(Donabedian v. Mercury Ins. Co.¿(2004) 116 Cal.App.4th 968, 994.)¿“A demurrer tests the pleading alone, and not¿on the evidence or facts alleged.” (E-Fab, Inc.¿v.¿Accountants, Inc. Servs.¿(2007) 153 Cal.App.4th 1308, 1315.) As such, the court assumes the truth of the complaint’s properly pleaded or implied factual allegations. (Id.) The only issue a demurrer is concerned with is whether the complaint, as it stands,¿states¿a cause of action. (Hahn, supra, 147 Cal.App.4th at 747.) Before filing a demurrer, demurring party¿is also required to¿meet and confer with the party who filed the pleading demurred to for the purposes of¿determining¿whether an agreement can be reached through a filing of an amended pleading that would resolve the objections to be raised in the demurrer. (See Code Civ. Proc., § 430.41.)¿

DISCUSSION  

Intentional Infliction of Emotional Distress

To state a cause of action for intentional infliction of emotional distress (IIED), the plaintiff must allege facts demonstrating, “(1) defendant engaged in extreme and outrageous conduct (conduct so extreme as to exceed all bounds of decency in a civilized community) with the intent to cause, or with reckless disregard to the probability of causing, emotional distress; and (2) as a result, plaintiff suffered extreme or severe emotional distress. Additionally, [i]t must be conduct directed at the plaintiff, or occur in the presence of the plaintiff of whom the defendant is aware.” (Berry v. Frazier (2023) 90 Cal.App.5th 1258, 1273 (Berry), internal quotation marks and citations omitted, italics in original.) “Whether a defendant’s conduct can reasonably be found to be outrageous is a question of law that must initially be determined by the court; if reasonable persons may differ, it is for the jury to determine whether the conduct was, in fact, outrageous. [Citation.]” (Berkley v. Dowds (2007) 152 Cal.App.4th 518, 534; but see Berry, supra, 90 Cal.App.5th at p. 1273 [“’[W]hether conduct is ‘outrageous’ is usually a question of fact.’ [Citation]”].)

Moving Parties demur to Plaintiff’s IIED claim on the grounds that Plaintiff does not state sufficient facts for such a claim and fails to allege any conduct that can be reasonably regarded as extreme and outrageous. Moving Parties contend that the alleged conduct arising from a single incident amounts to trivialities, insults, and threats that courts have consistently determined are not extreme and outrageous. Moving Parties contend that Boles’ alleged conduct of saying that he could “take [plaintiff] right now” or use of vulgar language is vague and inactionable and constitutes mere indignities or insults. Moving Parties also contend that Plaintiff does not allege facts showing that Shamim intended to or was going to slap Plaintiff.

In opposition, Plaintiff contends to have adequately pled a cause of action for IIED by describing Moving Parties’ extreme and outrageous conduct that caused Plaintiff severe emotional distress but also states that Plaintiff can provide additional conduct and context if necessary because their conduct is not limited to what is described in the Complaint. Plaintiff contends Moving Parties are members of the Board of Directors for Plaintiff’s homeowners association and therefore owed Plaintiff various fiduciary duties, which makes Plaintiff more susceptible to emotional distress from Moving Parties’ conduct. Plaintiff contends Moving Parties made physical threats in front of other association members which in one case required a third party to intervene to prevent a physical altercation. Plaintiff contends to be receiving treatment by a psychologist, dermatologist, and three allergists, and contends to have spent thousands of dollars on treatment to date.

The Court finds the Complaint fails to allege sufficient facts to state a cause of action for IIED. The extent of Plaintiff’s allegations are that Shamim said she wanted to slap Plaintiff as she moved toward Plaintiff until a neighbor intervened, Boles told Plaintiff he “could take [her] right now,” and that Defendants called Plaintiff a “bitch” in front of other homeowners and vendors. (Compl., ¶¶ 16, 39.) Moving Parties’ actions at most amount to insults, threats, and indignities, which are insufficient for purposes of IIED. “Liability for intentional infliction of emotional distress does not extend to mere insults, indignities, threats, annoyances, petty oppressions, or other trivialities.” (Hughes v. Pair (2009) 46 Cal.4th 1035, 1051, internal quotation marks and citation omitted.) The Complaint is otherwise devoid of allegations that demonstrate extreme and outrageous conduct to support Plaintiff’s IIED claim.

Accordingly, the Court SUSTAINS Moving Parties’ demurrer to the Fourth Cause of Action for intentional infliction of emotional distress with leave to amend.

Reclassification

Moving parties also contend the amount in controversy is well below the $35,000 threshold for limited matters and asks the Court to reclassify this matter as a limited action.

In opposition, Plaintiff contends the motion to reclassify should be denied because a verdict over the jurisdictional minimum is obtainable.

The Court finds the motion to reclassify unavailing. Given that the Court has sustained the demurrer with leave to amend, Plaintiff may be able to adequately allege facts stating a claim for IIED and thereby satisfy the $35,000 threshold for unlimited civil claims. (See Code Civ. Proc., § 86.)

CONCLUSION AND ORDER

The Court SUSTAINS Defendants Howard Boles and Susanna Shamim’s demurrer with 20 days’ leave to amend.

The Court DENIES the motion to reclassify.

Moving Parties to provide notice of this order.

Case Number: 26NNCV00989    Hearing Date: June 26, 2026    Dept: B

Hon. Lee S. Arian, Dept B 

MOTION TO QUASH

Hearing Date: 6/26/26¿ 

CASE NO./NAME: 26NNCV00989 JING XING FENG et al. vs. BAOLI WU et al.

Moving Party: Defendant Baoli Wu

Responding Party: None

Notice: Sufficient

Ruling: GRANTED

 

Background

 

On February 9, 2026, plaintiffs Jing Xing Feng and Rongxiang Feng (Plaintiffs) filed this action against defendant Baoli Wu (Defendant) arising out of a motor vehicle accident that occurred on November 26, 2024. Defendant was allegedly personally served as an individual, on March 31, 2026, at 7:26 p.m., at 3035 E Oak Knoll Loop, Ontario, CA 91761-3872, through a registered process server identified as Estevan Berrellez. Defendant now moves the Court for an order quashing service of summons.

Legal Standard

“‘Service of process, under longstanding tradition in our system of justice, is fundamental to any procedural imposition on a named defendant.’” (AO Alfa-Bank v. Yakovlev (2018) 21 Cal.App.5th 189, 202.) “To establish personal jurisdiction, compliance with statutory procedures for service of process is essential.” (Kremerman v. White (2021) 71 Cal.App.5th 358, 371.) A defendant’s knowledge of the action does not dispense with the statutory requirements for service of summons. (Kappel v. Bartlett (1988) 200 Cal.App.3d 1457, 1466.) 

“A defendant, on or before the last day of his or her time to plead or within any further time that the court may for good cause allow,” may move “to quash service of summons on the ground of lack of jurisdiction of the court over him or her.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 418.10(a)(1).) A defendant has 30 days after the service of the summons to file a responsive pleading. (Code Civ. Proc., § 412.20(a)(3).) 

“When a defendant challenges the court’s personal jurisdiction on the ground of improper service of process, ‘the burden is on the plaintiff to prove the existence of jurisdiction by proving, inter alia, the facts requisite to an effective service.’” (Summers v. McClanahan (2006) 140 Cal.App.4th 403, 413.) Filing of a proof of service that complies with the applicable statutory requirements creates a rebuttable presumption of proper service. (Am. Express Centurion Bank v. Zara (2011) 199 Cal.App.4th 383, 390.) 

Discussion

Defendant argues that service was improperly effectuated at 3035 E. Oak Knoll Loop, Ontario, California because Defendant does not reside at this address. (Motion, p. 1.) Defendant resides in China. (Ibid.) Defendant argues that service was effectuated at the home of Baojing Wang, Defendant’s estranged wife. (Ibid.) Defendant argues that because he has not been served the court lacks jurisdiction over him. (Motion, p. 3.)

Here, personal service was allegedly effectuated on Defendant at 3035 E. Oak Knoll Loop, Ontario, California. (Nguyen Decl., Exh. A “Proof of Service”.) However, Plaintiffs have not filed the proof of service.

Defendant’s estranged wife Baojing Wang declares that Defendant abandoned her and moved to parts unknown in China approximately three years ago. (Wang Decl., ¶ 6.) Boajing Wang declares that she resides at 3035 E. Oak Knoll Loop and states that Defendant was not present at the residence on March 31, 2026, when he was allegedly served. (Wang Decl., ¶¶ 7-9.) Boajing Wang also declares that she was not personally served with the Summons and Complaint at any time. (Wang Decl., ¶10.)

When a defendant files a motion to quash, the burden is on the plaintiff to establish that service of the summons and complaint was proper. (Summers v. McClanahan (2006) 140 Cal.App.4th 403, 413.) As Plaintiffs have failed to file an opposition to the motion, Plaintiffs have failed to meet Plaintiffs’ burden. As such, Defendant’s motion must be granted. Moreover, Defendant has submitted sufficient evidence to show the motion should be granted.

Accordingly, Defendant Baoli Wu’s motion to quash service of summons is granted.
